summary: Defines a new parameter, enumdi, for the tel URI so a phone-call system can show that an ENUM lookup was already done for a number. This keeps other network elements from repeating the query.

eli5.summary: Before calling a number you look it up in the phone book. This adds a small sticker saying, I already looked this up, so the next helper does not have to look again.

questions: what does enumdi mean in a tel uri
when should a voip element skip an enum query
subtitle: A small flag on a telephone-number URI that tells the next system an ENUM lookup has already been done.

tldr.problem: When a call is passed from one VoIP system to the next, each system may repeat the same ENUM lookup on the phone number, which wastes effort.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an optional ;enumdi parameter to the "tel" URI. A system that has already done the ENUM query attaches it, and a trusting receiver SHOULD NOT query ENUM again.
tldr.outcome: Redundant lookups can be skipped between trusting systems, but a forged or stripped flag can misroute a call, so the parameter is only trusted from trusted senders.

today: RFC 4759 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself needs no IANA action and points to the IANA "tel" URI parameter registry for registering parameters.

sections.title: Why a Dip Indicator Is Needed
sections.content:
VoIP network elements, including User Agent Servers and User Agent Clients, often handle an E.164 telephone number by querying ENUM (defined in RFC 3761) and using the set of NAPTR resource records that comes back.

If the query gives a result, the call is set up accordingly. If it does not, the element may ask another database or route the call to the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), possibly through another VoIP network element. That next element could repeat the same query for no benefit. The enumdi parameter on the "tel" URI (from RFC 3966) signals that an ENUM query has already been made, so the redundant query can be avoided.
sections.eli5: Imagine passing a note to a friend who would otherwise look up the same phone number again. A sticker on the note says the lookup is already done.

sections.title: The enumdi Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax uses the ABNF of RFC 4234 to extend the par production defined for the "tel" URI in RFC 3966. The new parameter is just the literal text ;enumdi, with no value.

It is optional, and it can appear at most once in any "tel" URI.
sections.eli5: The sticker is just one short word added to the end of the phone number, and you only stick it on once.

sections.title: Rules for Network Elements
sections.content:
Receiving the parameter. If a VoIP network element receives a "tel" URI with enumdi, it SHOULD NOT retrieve information for that number from ENUM in e164.arpa., even if it normally would. If the URI came from a trusted entity and is passed on, the element MUST pass it on unchanged, with the parameter in place. A recipient may reasonably still query ENUM if it has no trust relationship with the immediate sender. If the URI came from an untrusted entity, the recipient may either strip the parameter before sending it onwards, or do its own ENUM query and add the parameter accordingly.

Adding the parameter. If an element queries ENUM for a number and gets DNS error code 3 (NXDOMAIN), and then chooses to pass the call to another element using a "tel" URI, the enumdi parameter MUST be set.

URIs retrieved from ENUM. If the query returns a NAPTR record holding a "tel" URI with the same E.164 number, or one that already has enumdi, then passing that URI on requires the parameter to be set. If the retrieved URI holds a different E.164 number without the indicator, the element may query again or pass the request on, as local policy decides.

An ENUM domain provider may also choose to put the indicator in the "tel" URI of a NAPTR record. Following the rules above, that tells the client not to bother querying again.
sections.eli5: If a note has the sticker from someone you trust, you pass it along as it is. If you got it from a stranger, you may peel the sticker off or check the phone book yourself. If your own check found nothing, you add the sticker before passing it on.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In both examples, a network element called server.example.com receives tel:+441632960038 and queries the DNS for NAPTR records at 8.3.0.0.6.9.2.3.6.1.4.4.e164.arpa.. In the first it gets an NXDOMAIN error (code 3). In the second it gets the same "tel" URI back. In both cases it decides to route the call to the PSTN through another element called gw.example.com.

It then signals the next element with tel:+441632960038;enumdi, or, using the procedures of RFC 3261 section 19.1.6, with sip:+441632960038;enumdi@gw.example.com;user=phone.
sections.eli5: Whether the phone book had no entry or just repeated the same number, the helper marks the note with the sticker before handing it to the next helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If enumdi is illegally inserted while a message is en route, the call may be routed to the PSTN, which could incur unexpected charges or make a downstream VoIP element reject the call setup. Because many elements keep trust relationships with others, a recipient may ignore the parameter when the URI arrives from outside its trust boundary and make its own ENUM query, which avoids this attack.

Illegal removal is less of a problem: an extra ENUM query can fetch the routing information again and put the parameter back.

The RFC RECOMMENDS that protocols carrying the "tel" URI ensure message integrity between the two communicating network elements, so unauthorised changes can be detected.
sections.eli5: A prankster could stick the sticker on a note that should not have it, so you only believe stickers from friends you trust.
